title: Woody Allen's Tainted Legacy
tldr: Sam Morril and Joe Rogan take on the question of whether Woody Allen's filmography can be separated from the serious allegations made against him
Discussion of the specific claims in the Dylan Farrow case and what the original investigations did and didn't establish as fact
Morril argues the Allen vs. Farrow documentary presents one side compellingly but that the factual record is more contested than it appears
Conversation about the broader cultural question of what happens when you erase an artist's work and whether those decisions are applied consistently
Reflection on the intellectual honesty required to hold complicated views about artists whose personal conduct conflicts with their creative contributions
Morril brings his comedian's perspective to the absurdity of trying to establish clean moral verdicts in situations where the facts themselves remain disputed
recap:
Sam Morril sits down with Joe Rogan to dig into the complicated question of Woody Allen's place in film history after decades of controversy surrounding allegations made by his daughter Dylan Farrow. Morril, who has thought carefully about these questions from a comedian's perspective, brings a nuanced take to a conversation that most people either avoid entirely or reduce to a binary cancellation verdict.

Allen's filmography is unambiguous in one dimension: it's one of the most productive and critically acclaimed bodies of work in American cinema. Annie Hall, Manhattan, Hannah and Her Sisters, Crimes and Misdemeanors, and dozens of other films represent a consistent artistic vision that influenced generations of filmmakers and comedians alike. The question Morril and Joe grapple with is what to do with that body of work given the allegations that have been made.

Morril's approach is to separate the art from the artist as much as possible while acknowledging that complete separation is an intellectual dishonesty for many people. He's not here to exonerate Allen or to condemn him. He's here to think through the actual question of what it means that someone can produce work of genuine cultural value while also being accused of deeply serious things.

The conversation covers the specific details of what Allen was accused of and what the investigations at the time did and didn't conclude. Joe brings up the competing accounts and the way the Allen vs. Farrow documentary series renewed public interest in the story. Morril argues that the documentary presented one side compellingly but that the underlying factual picture is more contested than the film suggests.

They also talk about what happens to the broader culture when artists get erased. Allen's films continue to be watched and studied despite the controversy. The attempt to remove them from mainstream platforms has been partial and inconsistent, which raises questions about how these decisions get made and who makes them.

The clip closes with Morril reflecting on the personal difficulty of enjoying work made by people you've concluded did bad things, and whether that difficulty says something useful about the viewer as much as it does about the artist.
